report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is too strong. Evidence does **not** establish that simply “following a vegetarian diet” increases life expectancy compared with eating meat. It is an observational association in some populations, not a proven causal longevity effect.

The strongest counterevidence is a pooled UK analysis designed to compare vegetarians with health-conscious nonvegetarians: it found **similar all-cause mortality**. Thus, vegetarianism itself did not translate into a demonstrated survival advantage in that setting.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4691673/

There is supportive—but limited—evidence behind the view. In the Adventist Health Study-2, vegetarian dietary patterns were associated with lower mortality. But Adventists are an unusual, health-oriented group (with low smoking and alcohol use), and diet is self-selected. Statistical adjustment reduces, but cannot eliminate, confounding from exercise, income, healthcare, body weight, and other behaviors. The study is therefore evidence of association, not proof that removing meat causes a longer life.  
https://archive.connect.h1.co/article/718113551/

“Eating meat” is also too broad a comparison. WHO/IARC finds processed meat carcinogenic and red meat probably carcinogenic for colorectal cancer, but explicitly says its evaluation did **not** directly compare overall health risks of vegetarians with meat eaters. Risks depend on meat type, amount, replacement foods, and the overall dietary pattern.  
https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/cancer-carcinogenicity-of-the-consumption-of-red-meat-and-processed-meat

A well-planned vegetarian diet can be nutritionally adequate and may help prevent or treat some chronic diseases—but that is different from demonstrated longer life.  
https://www.jandonline.org/article/S2212-2672(16)31192-3/fulltext
